questions.prompt: What is the time budget per frame on a 60 Hz display before a scroll hitch happens?

options.explanation: Right. One second divided by 60 frames gives about 16.67 milliseconds per frame.
100 ms is the threshold where users notice a tap delay, not a 60 Hz frame budget.
250 ms is the default hang reporting threshold in Xcode tools.
Half a second would drop 30 frames in a row on a 60 Hz screen.

questions.prompt: How much time does each frame have on a 120 Hz ProMotion display?

options.explanation: 16.67 ms is the budget for a 60 Hz display, which is twice as long.
Right. At 120 frames per second, each frame must finish within 8.33 milliseconds.
40 ms would only achieve 25 frames per second, causing severe hitches.
120 is the refresh rate in hertz, not the frame duration in milliseconds.

questions.prompt: At what delay does a single user tap start to feel noticeably slow, before Apple tools report a hang?

options.explanation: 8.33 ms is the frame budget for 120 Hz scrolling, not a tap delay.
16.67 ms is one 60 Hz frame, which still feels instant for a single tap.
Right. Users begin noticing lag after 100 ms, while tools report hangs at 250 ms.
Five seconds is a long freeze, far above the 100 ms notice threshold.

questions.prompt: What is the main difference between a hang and a hitch?

options.text: A hang happens only in SwiftUI, while a hitch happens only in UIKit.
options.explanation: Both hangs and hitches can occur in UIKit and SwiftUI apps.

options.text: A hang happens in the GPU, while a hitch happens on a background thread.
options.explanation: Hangs happen when the main thread blocks; hitches happen in commit or render phases.

options.text: A hang lasts under 10 milliseconds, while a hitch lasts over 5 seconds.
options.explanation: Actually, hitches are short missed frames, while hangs last 250 ms or longer.

options.text: A hang freezes single actions, while a hitch drops frames during motion.
options.explanation: Right. Hangs delay taps or clicks, while hitches make scrolling or animations stutter.

questions.prompt: Which stage of the render loop runs on the main thread inside your app to update layout and layers?

options.explanation: Right. The Commit phase checks layout, SwiftUI body, and image decoding on the main thread.
The Render phase executes GPU commands in the separate system render server.
The Display phase shows the already-rendered pixels on the screen hardware.
The Event phase delivers touches and gestures before the Commit phase updates layout.

questions.prompt: Why does calling `UIImage.byPreparingForDisplay()` reduce scrolling hitches?

options.text: It saves a smaller JPEG file back to disk for the next launch.
options.explanation: byPreparingForDisplay creates a decoded image in memory and does not write to disk.

options.text: It skips the GPU render phase completely when drawing the cell.
options.explanation: The GPU still draws the prepared image to the screen.

options.text: It pauses scrolling gestures until every photo finishes loading.
options.explanation: It decodes images off the main thread without blocking touch or scroll events.

options.text: It decodes compressed image pixels ahead of time off the main thread.
options.explanation: Right. Decoding off the main thread avoids stalling the Commit phase when the cell appears.

questions.prompt: When downsampling with `CGImageSourceCreateThumbnailAtIndex(_:_:_:)`, what does `kCGImageSourceShouldCacheImmediately: true` do?

options.text: It decodes the downsampled bitmap right away on the current thread.
options.explanation: Right. When called on a background thread, immediate decoding avoids lazy main-thread decoding.

options.text: It waits to decode the image until `UIImageView` draws it on screen.
options.explanation: That is the default false behavior; setting true decodes pixels right away.

options.text: It rotates the thumbnail automatically using EXIF orientation tags.
options.explanation: kCGImageSourceCreateThumbnailWithTransform handles rotation; this key controls when decoding runs.

options.text: It keeps the full-size original image decoded alongside the thumbnail.
options.explanation: kCGImageSourceThumbnailMaxPixelSize limits the decoded image to the target pixel size.

questions.prompt: Why should you cache a single `DateFormatter` instead of creating a new one inside every scrolling cell?

options.text: Because `DateFormatter` only compiles inside a `static` property.
options.explanation: DateFormatter compiles anywhere, but recreating it per cell wastes frame time.

options.text: Because initializing `DateFormatter` is slow and burns main-thread frame time.
options.explanation: Right. Formatters parse locale data on setup, so reusing one keeps frame commits fast.

options.text: Because `DateFormatter` only works inside background actors.
options.explanation: DateFormatter can run on the main thread when reused cleanly.

options.text: Because creating a `DateFormatter` clears the text cache on every cell.
options.explanation: It does not clear other caches; its own setup cost causes the slowness.

questions.prompt: A 500 KB JPEG photo looks tiny on disk, yet loading 20 of them into small thumbnails spikes RAM and lags scrolling. Why?

options.text: UIKit keeps the compressed JPEG bytes in GPU memory without decoding.
options.explanation: The GPU needs raw uncompressed pixels, which takes far more RAM than the JPEG file.

options.text: Every `UIImageView` writes a second uncompressed copy back to disk.
options.explanation: The spike happens in RAM from decoded pixels, not from writing files to disk.

options.text: Memory depends on decoded pixel width and height, not compressed file size.
options.explanation: Right. A small JPEG can unpack into tens of megabytes of raw pixels.

options.text: Compressed JPEGs take more RAM per pixel than raw downsampled thumbnails.
options.explanation: Uncompressed raw pixels take much more memory than the compressed JPEG bytes on disk.

questions.prompt: Why does setting `layer.shadowOpacity` without `layer.shadowPath` hurt scrolling smoothness?

options.text: It forces Auto Layout to recalculate constraints on every scroll tick.
options.explanation: Shadow properties affect GPU rendering, not Auto Layout constraints.

options.text: It disables image decoding caches inside every visible `UIImageView`.
options.explanation: Shadow settings on CALayer do not turn off UIImageView image decoding.

options.text: It blocks the main thread from delivering touch and scroll events.
options.explanation: The Event phase still delivers touches; the delay happens in the Render phase.

options.text: The GPU must trace alpha pixels each frame using slow offscreen rendering.
options.explanation: Right. Giving Core Animation a shadowPath lets the GPU skip offscreen alpha tracing.

questions.prompt: In the render loop diagram, what happens when the Commit phase finishes after the 8.33 ms deadline?

options.text: The display repeats the previous frame, causing a visible hitch.
options.explanation: Right. Missing the commit deadline delays the GPU render, so the old frame stays on screen.

options.text: The GPU renders a blank white frame until the next scroll gesture.
options.explanation: The display shows the previous finished frame again, not a blank screen.

options.text: iOS pauses background threads so the main thread can catch up.
options.explanation: Background threads keep running; the missed frame simply appears late.

options.text: The watchdog kills the app after one missed 8.33 ms frame.
options.explanation: Watchdog kills happen after seconds of a blocked main thread, not a single dropped frame.

questions.prompt: With Swift 6.2+ Approachable Concurrency enabled, what happens when a `@MainActor` method calls an async helper marked `nonisolated` without `@concurrent`?

options.text: It always moves to a low-priority background thread.
options.explanation: That was Swift 6.0–6.1 behavior; under Approachable Concurrency, nonisolated async stays on caller actor.

options.text: It stays on `@MainActor`, so heavy CPU work there still blocks the UI.
options.explanation: Right. Under Approachable Concurrency, you need @concurrent to hop off @MainActor.

options.text: It refuses to compile unless you also mark the helper `@Sendable`.
options.explanation: nonisolated async functions compile cleanly; @concurrent controls executor hopping.

options.text: It creates a separate background `actor` automatically for each call.
options.explanation: It does not create a new actor; it inherits the caller's `@MainActor` isolation.

questions.prompt: Which Xcode runtime diagnostic warns you when the main thread waits on lower-priority work (priority inversion) or slow synchronous I/O?

options.explanation: Memory Graph Debugger inspects object references and retain cycles, not main-thread blocks.
View Hierarchy Debugger inspects 3D view layers and constraints, not thread priority inversions.
Right. Thread Performance Checker flags priority inversions and main-thread blocks while debugging.
Thread Sanitizer detects data races in memory, not priority inversions or synchronous I/O on main.

questions.prompt: Why is calling `DispatchQueue.main.sync` from code already running on the main thread a critical bug?

options.text: It silently skips the closure without running any code inside it.
options.explanation: It does not skip the closure; it blocks waiting for the main queue and deadlocks.

options.text: It moves the closure to a background thread and breaks UI safety.
options.explanation: DispatchQueue.main runs on the main thread, so calling sync from main waits on itself.

options.text: It forces the GPU to wait for one extra frame before drawing.
options.explanation: It freezes the main queue immediately rather than delaying by one frame.

options.text: The main queue waits for itself to finish, causing an immediate deadlock crash.
options.explanation: Right. A serial queue waiting synchronously on itself deadlocks and crashes.

questions.prompt: In 2–5 sentences, explain the difference between a hang and a hitch, including their key time thresholds.

rubric.criterion: Defines a hang as blocking the main thread on a single tap or action
Mentions hang thresholds: noticeable over 100 ms and reported by tools at 250 ms
Defines a hitch as a missed frame during scrolling or animation
Mentions frame budgets: 16.67 ms for 60 Hz and 8.33 ms for 120 Hz ProMotion

questions.modelAnswer: A hang happens when the main thread freezes during a single user action like a tap. Delays over 100 ms feel slow to users, and Apple tools report hangs starting at 250 ms. A hitch happens when a frame misses its deadline during scrolling or animation. The app must finish frame work in 16.67 ms at 60 Hz or 8.33 ms at 120 Hz ProMotion.

questions.prompt: In 2–5 sentences, name the four stages of the render loop and explain the difference between a commit hitch and a render hitch.

rubric.criterion: Names the four stages: Event, Commit, Render, and Display
Explains commit hitch: slow CPU/main-thread work in the app process (layout, body, decoding)
Explains render hitch: slow render server or GPU work (such as offscreen rendering)

questions.modelAnswer: The four stages of the render loop are Event, Commit, Render, and Display. A commit hitch happens inside your app process when main-thread CPU work such as layout or image decoding misses the commit deadline. A render hitch happens in the render server when the GPU takes too long to draw layers, often due to offscreen rendering passes.

questions.prompt: In 2–5 sentences, explain why full-size photos cause lag and high memory use in a scrolling list, and how to fix it.

rubric.criterion: Explains that memory depends on decoded pixel dimensions rather than compressed JPEG/PNG file size
Explains that default lazy decoding runs on the main thread during display
Recommends background downsampling or decoding (ImageIO CGImageSourceCreateThumbnailAtIndex or UIImage preparingForDisplay/byPreparingForDisplay/byPreparingThumbnail)

questions.modelAnswer: A small JPEG file can unpack (decompress) into tens of megabytes of raw pixels because memory depends on pixel width and height. By default, UIKit also decodes compressed images lazily on the main thread, which stalls scrolling. To fix this, downsample and decode images in the background to the target display size using ImageIO CGImageSourceCreateThumbnailAtIndex or UIImage.byPreparingThumbnail(ofSize:).

questions.prompt: In 2–5 sentences, explain how `nonisolated` async functions behave under Swift 6.2+ Approachable Concurrency and how `@concurrent` fixes main-thread stalls.

rubric.criterion: States that under Swift 6.2+ Approachable Concurrency, nonisolated async functions stay on the caller's actor
Explains that calling a heavy nonisolated async function from @MainActor therefore still runs on main
States that marking the function @concurrent forces it to hop off @MainActor onto the background thread pool

questions.modelAnswer: Under Swift 6.2+ Approachable Concurrency, a plain nonisolated async function runs on its caller's actor by default. If a @MainActor view model calls that function, heavy CPU work inside it still runs on the main thread and blocks the UI. Adding the @concurrent attribute forces Swift to hop off @MainActor and run the work on the background thread pool.
